name: Neural quantum states and volume-law entanglement
summary: Neural networks such as restricted Boltzmann machines and transformers serve as variational wavefunctions trained by variational Monte Carlo. An MPS's entanglement is capped at ln χ, but these networks can encode volume-law entanglement with polynomially many parameters (Deng, Li & Das Sarma 2017).

name: Born–Oppenheimer surfaces drive ab initio MD
summary: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation separates electrons from nuclei, with small parameter (m_e/M)^{1/4}. Ab initio and Car–Parrinello MD move classical nuclei on the electronic ground-state energy surface. The approximation fails at conical intersections, where nonadiabatic methods such as surface hopping take over.

name: Amplitude estimation speeds up Monte Carlo quadratically
summary: Amplitude amplification estimates an expectation value to error ε with O(1/ε) oracle calls, against O(1/ε²) samples classically (Montanaro 2015). It is the same 1/√N to 1/N jump as from the standard quantum limit to the Heisenberg limit.

name: Path-integral quantum Monte Carlo and the sign problem
summary: Slicing imaginary time turns the quantum partition function into a classical ensemble of ring polymers that Metropolis sampling can handle. This is exact for bosons, but fermion exchange produces negative weights. That is the sign problem, which is NP-hard in general (Troyer–Wiese 2005).

name: Trotter splitting: symplectic integrators and quantum gates
summary: Leapfrog and Strang symplectic integrators and split-step Schrödinger solvers use the same operator splitting that compiles e^{-iHt} into gates on a quantum computer. Higher-order Suzuki formulas and their commutator error bounds carry over directly.

name: Area-law entanglement makes MPS and DMRG efficient
summary: The Schmidt rank across any cut of a matrix product state is at most the bond dimension, so the entanglement entropy obeys S ≤ ln χ. Ground states of gapped 1D Hamiltonians obey an area law (Hastings 2007), so they compress efficiently, and entanglement growth sets the cost of time evolution.

name: Tensor-network contraction vs quantum-advantage claims
summary: After the random-circuit-sampling advantage claims (Arute et al. 2019), tensor-network contraction simulated the same circuits classically far faster than first estimated. The treewidth of a circuit's tensor network sets the classical cost, so tensor networks mark the moving boundary of quantum advantage.

name: Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument
summary: The 1927–35 Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument treated completeness and locality as philosophical questions. Bell (1964) turned them into testable inequalities, which is why foundations of QM is where history and philosophy meet the laboratory.

name: The quantum revolution, 1900–1927
summary: Blackbody radiation (Planck 1900), the photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905) and atomic spectra with the Bohr model (1913) led to matrix and wave mechanics (1925–26). Spectroscopy drove the experiments, and the episode is the standard case study of theory change.

name: No-go theorems as experimental metaphysics
summary: The Bell, Kochen–Specker and PBR theorems turn questions about hidden variables, locality and the reality of the wavefunction into constraints that experiments can test. Philosophy of physics now argues over which premise to give up, such as measurement independence or outcome independence.

name: Measurement problem and rival interpretations
summary: Unitary evolution and definite measurement outcomes conflict. Copenhagen, Everett's relative states, Bohmian mechanics, GRW collapse and QBism resolve this in different ways, and the meaning of Born-rule probability in many worlds is debated in both fields.

name: Typicality and ETH as foundations of statistical mechanics
summary: Philosophy of statistical mechanics asks why equilibrium ensembles work. Canonical typicality (almost every pure state of system plus bath has a thermal reduced state) and ETH (every energy eigenstate looks thermal) answer this for isolated quantum systems without ensembles or the ergodic hypothesis.

name: Eigenproblems and special functions of quantum mechanics
summary: Separation of variables, Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems and orthogonal polynomials (Hermite, Laguerre, Legendre) give the textbook spectra. Green's functions, contour integrals and asymptotic methods underpin perturbation theory, scattering and WKB.

name: Saddle points, Stokes lines and instantons
summary: Semiclassics evaluates the path integral by stationary phase or steepest descent. Airy functions join WKB solutions at turning points, Stokes phenomena control tunnelling exponents, and Wick rotation turns tunnelling into Euclidean instanton saddles.
map: \int\mathcal Dx\,e^{iS/\hbar}\approx\sum_{\rm cl}A_{\rm cl}\,e^{iS_{\rm cl}/\hbar},\ t\to-i\tau,\ \Gamma\propto e^{-S_E^{\rm inst}/\hbar}

name: Analytic S-matrix: poles, resonances, dispersion
summary: Causality makes partial-wave S-matrices analytic in complex momentum. Bound states are poles on the positive imaginary k axis and resonances are poles below the real axis that give Breit–Wigner peaks. The optical theorem and dispersion relations tie forward amplitudes to total cross sections.

name: Lippmann–Schwinger equation and the Born series
summary: The outgoing Helmholtz Green's function turns the Schrödinger equation into an integral equation. Iterating it gives the Born series, and its far-field limit gives the scattering amplitude f(θ).
map: \psi=\phi+G_0^{(+)}V\psi,\ G_0^{(+)}(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar^2}\frac{e^{ik|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Schmidt decomposition is the singular value decomposition
summary: Arrange a bipartite pure state's amplitudes as a matrix and its SVD is the Schmidt form. The squared singular values are the eigenvalues of the reduced state, so entanglement entropy and Schmidt rank are matrix invariants. The same SVD truncation drives DMRG.

name: Dirac notation and operator algebra
summary: The working tools of QM are linear-algebra results: commutators and simultaneous diagonalisation, unitary changes of basis, ladder-operator algebras, and rigged Hilbert spaces for the continuous spectra of position and momentum.

name: Spectral theorem as the measurement postulate
summary: States are rays in a Hilbert space and observables are self-adjoint operators. The spectral theorem supplies the possible outcomes (eigenvalues) and projectors that give the Born rule and state update. Gleason's theorem shows this is the only consistent probability measure for dimension ≥ 3.

name: Berry phase as holonomy of a U(1) connection
summary: The Berry connection is a connection on the line bundle of eigenstates over parameter space. Its curvature 2-form integrates to the Berry phase, and over closed surfaces to integer Chern numbers (Simon 1983). The quantum geometric tensor combines the Fubini–Study metric with the Berry curvature.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Quantum-limited amplifiers for qubit readout
summary: Dispersive readout of superconducting qubits needs Josephson parametric or travelling-wave amplifiers that work near the Caves bound: a phase-insensitive amplifier must add at least half a quantum of noise. The same SQUID and Josephson technology reads out cryogenic detectors.

name: Cryogenic sensors as single-photon detectors
summary: Cryogenic sensors and the noise analysis of instrumentation have become quantum-optics hardware. Transition-edge sensors resolve photon number with about 95% efficiency, and superconducting nanowire detectors reach about 98% efficiency with few-picosecond jitter. Dark counts and dead time are the other figures of merit.

name: Quantum Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
summary: Optimising the classical Cramér–Rao bound over all quantum measurements gives the quantum Fisher information (Braunstein–Caves 1994). N independent probes give F_Q = N, the standard quantum limit; entangled probes reach up to N², the Heisenberg limit.

name: Clock uncertainty budgets and Allan deviation
summary: Clock accuracy is quoted as a GUM-style budget of Type B systematic shifts (blackbody, Zeeman, Stark, motional) added in quadrature. Stability is quoted as the Allan deviation, which quantum projection noise ultimately limits. This is how the Al+/Hg+ ratio reached the 17th decimal place.
sources: Rosenband et al. (2008). "Frequency Ratio of Al+and Hg+Single-Ion Optical Clocks; Metrology at the 17th Decimal Place". *Science* 319, 1808. [doi:10.1126/science.1154622](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1154622)

name: Rotation symmetry labels states and selection rules
summary: Rotational invariance of H makes j and m good quantum numbers. The Wigner–Eckart theorem splits every tensor-operator matrix element into a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient times a reduced element, which gives the dipole selection rules.

name: Atomic parity violation and electron EDM searches
summary: Z-boson exchange mixes S and P states, so the forbidden Cs 6S–7S transition gains a parity-odd amplitude that measures the weak charge Q_W (Wood et al. 1997). Electron-EDM searches in heavy atoms and polar molecules test T, and hence CP, violation; the best bound is |d_e| < 4.1×10^{-30} e·cm (JILA HfF+, 2023).

name: PT symmetry and exceptional points
summary: A non-Hermitian Hamiltonian that commutes with the antiunitary PT operator has a real spectrum while the symmetry is unbroken. At the breaking threshold, eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce at an exceptional point: H becomes a non-diagonalisable Jordan block, the eigenvalues meet at a square-root branch point, and the splitting grows as √ε.
sources: Bender & Boettcher (1998). "Real Spectra in Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians Having P T Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 5243. [doi:10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243)

name: Dyson's threefold way fixes chaotic level statistics
summary: Spectra of chaotic systems follow random-matrix statistics (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit 1984). Antiunitary symmetry picks the ensemble: GOE if T² = +1, GUE if T is broken, GSE if T² = −1. The level-repulsion exponent β is the diagnostic.

name: Kramers degeneracy from T² = −1 for half-integer spin
summary: Time reversal is antiunitary and acts on spin as Θ = e^{-iπS_y/ħ}K, so Θ² = (−1)^{2S}. With an odd number of electrons, every level is at least doubly degenerate unless a magnetic field breaks T. This is the origin of the protected Kramers pairs in topological insulators.

name: Spin is a projective representation of SO(3)
summary: Angular-momentum operators obey the su(2) algebra, whose irreducible representations give j = 0, 1/2, 1, …. Half-integer spin exists because SU(2) double-covers SO(3): a 2π rotation multiplies a spinor by −1, as seen in neutron interferometry.

name: Hidden SO(4) symmetry of the hydrogen atom
summary: On bound states, the angular momentum L and the scaled Runge–Lenz vector K generate so(4) ≅ su(2)⊕su(2). Pauli (1926) used this to obtain the Bohr levels algebraically, and it explains the n² degeneracy across ℓ. SU(3) plays the same role for the 3D isotropic oscillator.

name: Quantum Noether: conserved generators commute with H
summary: By Wigner's theorem, symmetries act as unitary or antiunitary operators. If a continuous symmetry e^{-iθG/ħ} leaves H invariant, then [G,H] = 0 and the distribution of G is conserved. This is the operator form of Noether's theorem: momentum from translations, J from rotations, charge from U(1).

name: BEC breaks U(1); Bogoliubov phonon is the Goldstone mode
summary: The condensate order parameter ψ = √n e^{iθ} breaks the global phase symmetry that goes with atom-number conservation. The gapless Bogoliubov sound mode is the Goldstone boson, and its sound speed sets the Landau critical velocity for superfluid flow.

name: Time crystals break time-translation symmetry
summary: Wilczek's (2012) equilibrium time crystal is ruled out by the Watanabe–Oshikawa no-go theorem. Instead, periodically driven many-body systems, which conserve quasienergy rather than energy, break the discrete Floquet time-translation symmetry and respond at period 2T. Many-body localization or prethermalization protects this order, which has been seen with trapped ions, NV centres and superconducting qubits.

name: The SI second is a caesium hyperfine frequency
summary: Since 1967 the second has been defined by fixing the Cs ground-state hyperfine frequency. Time and frequency are the most precisely realised SI quantities, and the metre is traced to them through the fixed value of c.

name: Unitary Fermi gas: universality from a missing scale
summary: At a Feshbach resonance the scattering length diverges and drops out, leaving density as the only scale. Dimensional analysis then forces every observable to be a universal number times its free-Fermi-gas value, the Bertsch parameter ξ being one example. Dilute neutron matter shares the same universality.

name: AMO measurements determine α and m_e for CODATA
summary: The fine-structure constant comes from atom-recoil interferometry (h/m for Cs and Rb) and from the Penning-trap electron g-factor combined with QED. These AMO inputs dominate the CODATA values of α, R∞ and m_e, and the ~5σ gap between the Cs and Rb values remains unresolved.

name: Clock ratios test the constancy of α and m_p/m_e
summary: Different transitions depend on α and μ = m_p/m_e with different sensitivities, so repeated ratios between clocks (Al+/Hg+, Yb+ E3/E2, Cs/Sr) bound present-day drifts at the ~10^{-18} per year level. The same ratios search for ultralight dark matter, which would make the constants oscillate.
sources: Rosenband et al. (2008). "Frequency Ratio of Al+and Hg+Single-Ion Optical Clocks; Metrology at the 17th Decimal Place". *Science* 319, 1808. [doi:10.1126/science.1154622](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1154622)

name: Hydrogen spectroscopy, R∞ and the proton radius
summary: The Rydberg constant and the proton charge radius are fitted together to hydrogen and deuterium transition frequencies. The muonic-hydrogen Lamb shift (2010) gave a radius 4% smaller. The puzzle eased once newer hydrogen measurements and CODATA 2018/2022 moved to about 0.84 fm.

name: Optical clocks and redefining the second
summary: Optical lattice and ion clocks now beat the Cs primary standard by about 100×. The CIPM roadmap therefore plans an optical redefinition of the second around 2030, continuing the 2019 move to defining units by fixed constants.

name: Lagrangian generates quantum propagation (Dirac–Feynman)
summary: Dirac (1933) noticed that the short-time quantum propagator behaves like exp(iS/ħ), with S the classical action. Feynman built the path integral on this, which made the Lagrangian rather than the Hamiltonian the primary object of quantum dynamics.
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Bohmian mechanics as quantum Hamilton–Jacobi theory
summary: With ψ=R e^{iS/ħ}, the Schrödinger equation is exactly a Hamilton–Jacobi equation plus Bohm's quantum potential Q (Madelung 1927, Bohm 1952). De Broglie–Bohm theory has particles move along v=∇S/m, the characteristics of this equation, which gives a deterministic hidden-variable interpretation.
breaks: For many particles Q is nonlocal in configuration space and does not weaken as |ψ| shrinks. The motion is first-order, so initial momenta are not free. The mathematics is exact, but the interpretation is contested.
sources: Bohm (1952). "A Suggested Interpretation of the Quantum Theory in Terms of 'Hidden' Variables. I". *Phys. Rev.* 85, 166. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.85.166](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.85.166)

name: WKB: Schrödinger reduces to Hamilton–Jacobi
summary: Writing ψ=A e^{iS/ħ} turns the Schrödinger equation into the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at leading order, plus a continuity equation for A. Quantizing the action variables J=∮p dq gives the Bohr–Sommerfeld and EBK rules. Ehrenfest argued that action variables were the right quantities to quantize because they are adiabatic invariants.
breaks: It breaks down at turning points and caustics, where A diverges (Airy matching and the Maslov 1/2 repair this), and wherever the de Broglie wavelength changes quickly.
sources: Schrödinger (1926). "Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem". *Ann. Phys.* 384, 361. [doi:10.1002/andp.19263840404](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19263840404)

name: Hannay angle: classical counterpart of the Berry phase
summary: When an integrable system's parameters are cycled adiabatically, the action J stays invariant but the conjugate angle picks up a geometric shift, the Hannay angle. Berry showed that it is the semiclassical limit of the Berry phase of the quantum state with the same quantum number.
breaks: It requires invariant tori. Chaotic systems have no angle variables, and their adiabatic response takes a different form (geometric magnetism, Berry–Robbins).
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Hamilton's principal function as the semiclassical phase
summary: In the stationary-phase evaluation of the path integral, the phase is Hamilton's principal function S(x_b,x_a,t), which generates the classical time-evolution map. The prefactor is its mixed second derivative (the Van Vleck–Gutzwiller propagator), and caustics of the classical family add Maslov phases.
breaks: It fails near caustics and beyond the Ehrenfest time, where classical paths proliferate (chaos). It also fails where no real classical path exists: tunnelling needs complex or Euclidean paths.

name: Epistemically restricted Liouville mechanics ≈ Gaussian QM
summary: Classical Liouville mechanics with an uncertainty-like limit on what can be known about phase-space points reproduces Gaussian quantum mechanics, including entanglement and teleportation (Bartlett, Rudolph and Spekkens). The genuinely nonclassical resource therefore lies outside it: contextuality, which is equivalent to negativity of the Wigner function.
breaks: The model cannot reproduce non-Gaussian states or operations, Bell violations or Kochen–Specker contextuality, because it is a noncontextual hidden-variable model by construction.

name: Poisson bracket → commutator (canonical quantization)
summary: Dirac recognized that Heisenberg's commutators obey the algebra of classical Poisson brackets, so quantization replaces {A,B} with [Â,B̂]/iħ. Hamilton's equations then become the Heisenberg equations of motion, and the Liouville equation becomes the von Neumann equation for the density matrix.
map: \{A,B\}\to\tfrac{1}{i\hbar}[\hat A,\hat B];\ \dot A=\{A,H\}\to\dot{\hat A}=\tfrac{i}{\hbar}[\hat H,\hat A];\ \partial_t\rho=\{H,\rho\}\to i\hbar\partial_t\hat\rho=[\hat H,\hat\rho]
breaks: The map is not exact for all observables. The Groenewold–van Hove theorem rules out a consistent quantization of all polynomials, so operator ordering is ambiguous at O(ħ²).
sources: Heisenberg (1925). "Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen". *Z. Phys.* 33, 879. [doi:10.1007/BF01328377](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01328377)

name: Phase-space QM: Liouville flow to Wigner–Moyal
summary: The Wigner function is a quasi-probability on classical phase space that evolves by the Liouville equation with the Poisson bracket replaced by the Moyal bracket. Quantum optics describes light with Wigner, Husimi-Q and Glauber–Sudarshan-P distributions; Wigner negativity or a singular P function marks a nonclassical state.
map: \partial_tW=\{H,W\}_{\star}=\{H,W\}+O(\hbar^2\,\partial^3H\,\partial^3W);\ \ W\ \text{follows the classical flow exactly if}\ H\ \text{is quadratic}
breaks: W can be negative, so it is not a probability. Moyal corrections at O(ħ²) appear for anharmonic Hamiltonians, so classical Liouville flow is exact only for quadratic H (linear optics).
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)

name: Circuit quantization from the node-flux Lagrangian
summary: Superconducting circuits are quantized by writing a Lagrangian in node fluxes, with capacitive energy as kinetic energy and inductive and Josephson energy as potential energy. A Legendre transform makes the charges the conjugate momenta, and one then imposes [Φ,Q]=iħ. Kirchhoff loops and flux quantization act as holonomic constraints.
breaks: Dissipative and non-Lagrangian elements (resistors, nonreciprocal gyrators) need a bath or an extended treatment. Offset charges and compact phase variables need care.

name: Least action as stationary phase
summary: As ħ→0, Hamilton's principle δS=0 is the stationary-phase condition of the sum over e^{iS/ħ}: only paths near the classical one interfere constructively, just as Fermat's principle emerges from Huygens' wave optics. In imaginary time the same logic picks out minima of the Euclidean action (instantons).
map: \hbar\to0:\ \int\mathcal{D}x\,e^{iS/\hbar}\ \text{dominated by}\ \delta S=0\ \Leftrightarrow\ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Madelung: condensates as inviscid, irrotational fluids
summary: With ψ=√n e^{iθ}, the Gross–Pitaevskii equation becomes the continuity and Euler equations of an inviscid, irrotational fluid with velocity v=ħ∇θ/m, plus a quantum-pressure term. Kelvin's circulation theorem becomes the topological quantization of circulation around vortex lines, and the Landau criterion sets the critical velocity for dissipation.
map: \mathbf v=\tfrac{\hbar}{m}\nabla\theta;\ \ m\partial_t\mathbf v=-\nabla\big(\tfrac12mv^2+V+gn+Q\big);\ \ \oint\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf l=\tfrac{h}{m}\ell,\ \ell\in\mathbb Z
breaks: The fluid picture fails inside vortex cores and below the healing length ξ, where quantum pressure dominates. At finite temperature a normal component adds viscosity (the two-fluid model).

name: Low-Re swimming as a gauge holonomy (Shapere–Wilczek)
summary: At low Reynolds number, a swimmer's net displacement after a cyclic stroke depends only on the loop traced in shape space: it is the holonomy of a gauge connection, as with the Berry phase. For small strokes the displacement is the curvature times the enclosed area, so reciprocal strokes, which enclose no area, cannot swim (Purcell's scallop theorem).
map: \Delta\mathbf x=\oint_{\rm stroke}\mathcal A(s)\,ds\approx\iint\mathcal F\,da,\ \ \mathcal F=d\mathcal A+\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal A;\ \ \text{reciprocal stroke}\Rightarrow\Delta\mathbf x=0
breaks: The connection is non-abelian (it mixes rotations and translations) and comes from the reciprocity of Stokes flow, not from a quantum state. The effect is purely kinematic and dissipative.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Quantum turbulence: Kolmogorov cascades in vortex tangles
summary: Tangles of quantized vortices in superfluid helium and atomic condensates reproduce Kolmogorov's k^{-5/3} spectrum at scales larger than the intervortex spacing. Below that scale, energy moves through vortex reconnections and Kelvin-wave cascades. 2D condensates show inverse cascades and Onsager's negative-temperature vortex clusters.
breaks: There is no viscosity: energy is dissipated by phonon emission and reconnections at the smallest scales. Quantized circulation also imposes a discrete vortex scale that classical turbulence lacks.

name: Kepler–hydrogen: Runge–Lenz vector and hidden SO(4)
summary: The conserved Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, which keeps Kepler orbits closed (Bertrand's theorem), enlarges the symmetry of the 1/r problem from SO(3) to SO(4). Pauli (1926) used its quantum version to derive the hydrogen spectrum algebraically, and the same symmetry explains hydrogen's accidental n² degeneracy.
map: \mathbf A=\mathbf p\times\mathbf L-mk\,\hat{\mathbf r};\ \ \mathfrak{so}(4):\ E_n=-\frac{mk^2}{2\hbar^2n^2},\ g_n=n^2\ \ (k=Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0)
breaks: Any departure from 1/r (relativity, core penetration, spin–orbit coupling) breaks SO(4). Classically the orbits then precess; quantum mechanically the ℓ-levels split.

name: Rutherford scattering: classical = quantum for 1/r
summary: The Coulomb differential cross section comes out the same from classical orbits, from the first Born approximation and from the exact quantum solution. This accident of the 1/r potential is why Rutherford's classical analysis could reveal the nucleus. For other potentials, features of the classical deflection function (rainbows, glories, orbiting) reappear as stationary-phase points of the partial-wave sum (Ford–Wheeler).
breaks: In general the classical and quantum cross sections differ. Diffraction and shadow scattering make the quantum total cross section of a hard sphere twice its geometric value at high energy, and identical-particle (Mott) interference has no classical analogue.
sources: Born (1926). "Zur Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge". *Z. Phys.* 37, 863. [doi:10.1007/BF01397477](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01397477)

name: Symplectic splitting ↔ Trotter–Suzuki Hamiltonian simulation
summary: Long-term N-body integration splits H into exactly solvable flows (leapfrog, Wisdom–Holman, Yoshida–Suzuki compositions). Digital quantum simulation uses the same product formulas for e^{-iHt}. The error is set by nested Poisson brackets in the classical case and nested commutators in the quantum case.
breaks: Classical integrators preserve symplecticity, which keeps the energy error bounded; quantum product formulas are exactly unitary. Quantum cost is counted in gates, and the error scales with commutator norms.

name: Ehrenfest theorem: Newton's second law on average
summary: Expectation values obey m d²⟨x⟩/dt² = −⟨V′(x)⟩, Newton's second law for the centroid of a wave packet. The centroid follows the classical trajectory only when ⟨V′(x)⟩=V′(⟨x⟩): for at most quadratic potentials, or for packets narrow compared with the scale over which the force changes.
map: m\frac{d^2\langle\hat x\rangle}{dt^2}=-\langle V'(\hat x)\rangle\approx-V'(\langle\hat x\rangle)\ \ (\text{exact iff}\ V'''=0)
breaks: Wave-packet spreading and anharmonicity spoil the agreement after the Ehrenfest time. The theorem does not imply classical behaviour of individual measurement outcomes.

name: Atom interferometers as gravimeters and Sagnac gyroscopes
summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers turn the classical kinematics of free fall and rotating frames into matter-wave phases. The gravity phase k_eff g T² underlies atomic gravimeters, and the Sagnac phase from Earth's rotation makes atom gyroscopes; when rotation is not the target, the Coriolis terms must be compensated.
breaks: For equal area, the matter-wave Sagnac phase exceeds the optical one by mc²/ħω ~ 10^10, but atom interferometers enclose far smaller areas.

name: Rotation as synthetic magnetism: Coriolis ↔ Lorentz
summary: In a frame rotating at Ω the Coriolis force has the form of a Lorentz force with qB=2mΩ. Rotating condensates therefore form triangular vortex lattices, like type-II superconductors in a field, and as Ω approaches the trap frequency they enter the lowest-Landau-level regime, which resembles the quantum Hall effect.
breaks: The centrifugal term weakens confinement and frees the gas as Ω→ω⊥, which has so far kept rotating gases out of deep fractional-quantum-Hall states. Laser-induced gauge fields avoid this problem.
sources: Bloch, Dalibard & Zwerger (2008). "Many-body physics with ultracold gases". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 80, 885. [arXiv:0704.3011](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.3011)

name: Foucault pendulum precession as a holonomy
summary: After one sidereal day, the Foucault pendulum's plane of swing has turned by the solid angle enclosed by its circle of latitude, a holonomy of parallel transport on a sphere. The same geometry gives a spin's Berry phase as −m times the solid angle traced by the field direction.
breaks: Foucault's pendulum transports a real vector (an SO(2) holonomy of the sphere's Levi-Civita connection). Berry's phase is a U(1) phase of a complex state; it scales with m and shows up only relative to another path.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: BGS conjecture: classical chaos ↔ random-matrix spectra
summary: Whether the classical limit is integrable or chaotic fixes the quantum level statistics: Poisson spacings for integrable motion (Berry–Tabor), Wigner–Dyson level repulsion for fully chaotic motion (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit), and intermediate statistics for mixed KAM phase spaces. Periodic-orbit theory explains why.
map: P_{\rm int}(s)=e^{-s}\ \ \text{vs}\ \ P_{\rm GOE}(s)\approx\frac{\pi s}{2}e^{-\pi s^2/4}
breaks: There are exceptions. Arithmetic chaotic systems, such as billiards on special constant-curvature surfaces, show Poisson statistics, and non-generic integrable systems such as harmonic oscillators do not follow Berry–Tabor.
sources: Bohigas, Giannoni & Schmit (1984). "Characterization of Chaotic Quantum Spectra and Universality of Level Fluctuation Laws". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 1. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1)

name: Bosonic Josephson junction: pendulum bifurcation, self-trapping
summary: The mean-field dynamics of a condensate in a double well, in population imbalance z and relative phase φ, is that of a nonrigid pendulum. Raising the interaction parameter Λ through a bifurcation produces macroscopic quantum self-trapping, observed with rubidium in 2005; the large atom number N plays the role of 1/ħ.
breaks: At finite N, quantum fluctuations cause collapse and revival and tunnelling between the two self-trapped states. The classical pendulum is only the N→∞ limit.

name: Period doubling vs discrete time-crystalline order
summary: Driven dissipative classical systems (Faraday waves, parametrically driven pendula, period-doubling bifurcations) respond robustly at twice the drive period. Discrete time crystals are the many-body quantum version: a period-doubled response that resists drive imperfections and is long-range ordered, seen in trapped ions, NV centres and superconducting processors.
breaks: Classical period doubling relies on dissipation into an attractor. Closed quantum time crystals must avoid Floquet heating through many-body localization or prethermalization, and their rigidity is a many-body effect, although classical many-body time crystals in coupled dissipative oscillators have been proposed.

name: Chaos, Ehrenfest time and decoherence
summary: Classical chaos stretches a wave packet exponentially, so an isolated chaotic system stops tracking its classical counterpart after the Ehrenfest time, ~λ⁻¹ln(S/ħ), which for Saturn's moon Hyperion is only decades. Environmental decoherence restores the classical Liouville limit. Zurek and Paz argued that the entropy production rate then becomes independent of ħ and is set by the Lyapunov exponents.
breaks: Entropy production at the Lyapunov rate holds in an intermediate range of decoherence strength and is supported numerically, not proven in general.
sources: Zurek (2003). "Decoherence, einselection, and the quantum origins of the classical". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 715. [arXiv:quant-ph/0105127](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0105127)

name: Lyapunov exponent ↔ OTOC growth and the chaos bound
summary: The out-of-time-order correlator is the quantum version of the squared Poisson bracket {x(t),p}², which measures sensitivity to initial conditions. In semiclassical systems it therefore grows as e^{2λt}, with λ the classical Lyapunov exponent, until the scrambling time. Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford bounded the quantum rate by 2πk_BT/ħ.
breaks: Exponential OTOC growth lasts only until t~λ⁻¹ln(1/ħ_eff). It is absent in many chaotic systems with small local Hilbert spaces (spin-1/2 chains), and unstable saddle points in integrable systems produce it without chaos. The thermal bound has no classical counterpart.
sources: Maldacena, Shenker & Stanford (2016). "A bound on chaos". *JHEP* 08, 106. [arXiv:1503.01409](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01409)

name: Ergodicity: classical mixing vs eigenstate thermalization
summary: Classical statistical mechanics rests on chaotic, mixing motion on the energy shell. Its quantum replacement, the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, holds that individual eigenstates of chaotic Hamiltonians already look thermal; Srednicki derived it from Berry's random-wave conjecture for the eigenfunctions of classically chaotic systems.
breaks: ETH concerns eigenstates, not trajectories, and does not need a classical limit (spin-1/2 chains obey it). Many-body localization and quantum many-body scars, named after Heller's periodic-orbit scars, violate it.
sources: Deutsch (1991). "Quantum statistical mechanics in a closed system". *Phys. Rev. A* 43, 2046. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.43.2046](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.43.2046)
Srednicki (1994). "Chaos and quantum thermalization". *Phys. Rev. E* 50, 888. [arXiv:cond-mat/9403051](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9403051)

name: Kicked rotor: chaotic diffusion vs dynamical localization
summary: Chirikov's standard map loses its last KAM torus near K≈0.97, after which momentum diffuses without bound. The quantum kicked rotor follows this diffusion only up to a break time and then localizes in momentum. Fishman, Grempel and Prange mapped this dynamical localization onto Anderson localization, and it was observed with cold atoms in pulsed optical standing waves.
map: p_{n+1}=p_n+K\sin\theta_n,\ \ \theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+p_{n+1};\ \ \langle p^2\rangle_{\rm cl}\approx\tfrac{K^2}{2}n\ \ \text{vs quantum saturation after}\ t^*\propto D/\hbar_{\rm eff}^2
breaks: Localization is a quantum interference effect with no classical counterpart. Noise or decoherence restores classical diffusion, and at quantum resonances (rational ħ_eff/4π) the energy grows ballistically.

name: Torus quantization (EBK) and Gutzwiller's periodic-orbit sum
summary: Einstein (1917) quantized the actions on invariant tori and noted that the rule fails when the tori are destroyed. KAM theory says which tori survive. For fully chaotic motion, Gutzwiller's trace formula, a stationary-phase evaluation of the path integral, replaces torus quantization with a sum over unstable periodic orbits.
breaks: Mixed phase spaces need both pictures, plus tunnelling between regular and chaotic regions. The periodic-orbit sum diverges because the number of orbits grows exponentially, so it has to be resummed.

name: Gross–Pitaevskii = NLS: matter-wave solitons
summary: In a 1D waveguide the Gross–Pitaevskii equation reduces to the integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Repulsive condensates therefore carry dark solitons and attractive ones bright solitons and soliton trains, all seen in BECs between 1999 and 2002. The same equation governs solitons in optical fibres.
breaks: Transverse confinement and the trap break integrability. In 2D and 3D, dark solitons decay into vortices through the snake instability, and attractive 3D condensates collapse. Beyond mean field, the quantum NLS (Lieb–Liniger) is solved by the Bethe ansatz.

name: Integrability blocks thermalization: Lax charges and GGE
summary: Classical integrable systems carry an extensive set of conserved quantities generated by a Lax pair. That is why soliton collisions are elastic and FPUT-type lattices recur instead of equilibrating. Quantum integrable systems (Lieb–Liniger, the quantum NLS) likewise fail to thermalize and relax to a generalized Gibbs ensemble, as the quantum Newton's cradle experiment showed.
breaks: Quantum conserved charges constrain relaxation only if they are local or quasi-local. In both the classical and quantum cases, weak integrability breaking gives prethermal plateaus and eventually thermalization.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Harmonic oscillator: normal modes to ladder operators
summary: Any small oscillation about equilibrium, once reduced to normal modes, quantizes to the quantum harmonic oscillator. The classical complex amplitude becomes the ladder operator a, giving the equally spaced spectrum ħω(n+1/2) that is the template for phonons, photons and quasiparticles.
breaks: The zero-point energy ħω/2 and the discrete exchange of energy have no classical counterpart. The equal level spacing is why the classical and quantum frequencies coincide.

name: Bogoliubov transformation: normal modes of a condensate
summary: Linearizing about the condensate gives a quadratic bosonic Hamiltonian that a Bogoliubov transformation diagonalizes. This is normal-mode analysis with a symplectic rather than orthogonal transformation, and it yields phonon-like quasiparticles. In traps, the low-lying collective modes (the Kohn dipole mode at the trap frequency, breathing and quadrupole modes) are measured like classical normal modes.
breaks: Classical normal-mode analysis has no counterpart to the u,v mixing of creation and annihilation operators, which produces quantum depletion and a two-mode-squeezed ground state.

name: Ion-crystal normal modes as the quantum bus
summary: Ions in a linear Paul trap form a Coulomb crystal whose small oscillations split into normal modes (centre of mass, breathing, ...). These quantized modes mediate the Cirac–Zoller and Mølmer–Sørensen entangling gates and set the effective spin–spin couplings used in trapped-ion quantum simulation.

name: Ring-polymer isomorphism for quantum statistics
summary: Discretizing the imaginary-time path integral maps a quantum particle at temperature T onto a classical ring polymer of P beads joined by harmonic springs. Classical molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo (PIMD, RPMD) can then compute quantum equilibrium properties, and the ring's normal modes are used to integrate and thermostat it efficiently.
breaks: It is exact only for equilibrium statics. Real-time quantum dynamics (RPMD) is an approximation, and fermions bring a sign problem.

name: Vacuum Rabi splitting vs classical normal-mode splitting
summary: Two coupled resonators show an avoided crossing of width 2g, and the classical strong-coupling criterion g>κ,γ is the same as the quantum one. The single-excitation vacuum Rabi doublet of cavity QED matches this classical normal-mode splitting quantitatively.
breaks: The anharmonic √n ladder of a two-level emitter (photon blockade, collapse and revival, number-dependent Rabi frequencies) has no linear classical counterpart. Only that ladder proves quantum strong coupling.
sources: Jaynes & Cummings (1963). "Comparison of quantum and semiclassical radiation theories with application to the beam maser". *Proc. IEEE* 51, 89. [doi:10.1109/PROC.1963.1664](https://doi.org/10.1109/PROC.1963.1664)

Wallraff et al. (2004). "Strong coupling of a single photon to a superconducting qubit using circuit quantum electrodynamics". *Nature* 431, 162. [doi:10.1038/nature02851](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02851)

name: Field quantization = quantizing normal modes
summary: Expanding the electromagnetic field in cavity normal modes turns it into a set of uncoupled harmonic oscillators, just as normal-mode analysis decouples a chain of masses. Quantizing each mode gives photons, Planck's spectrum and vacuum fluctuations.
map: H=\sum_k\hbar\omega_k\big(a_k^\dagger a_k+\tfrac12\big),\quad \hat{\mathbf E}(\mathbf r)=\sum_k\mathcal E_k\big(a_k\mathbf u_k(\mathbf r)+\mathrm{h.c.}\big)
breaks: Classical equipartition, k_BT per mode, gives the Rayleigh–Jeans catastrophe. Quantizing the mode energies removes it.

name: Optical molasses and the MOT as a damped oscillator
summary: Doppler cooling produces a velocity-dependent force F=−βv (hence 'optical molasses'), and the magneto-optical trap adds a restoring force −κx, so trapped atoms are damped, usually overdamped, harmonic oscillators. Random photon recoils supply the fluctuating force, and fluctuation–dissipation sets the Doppler limit.
map: m\ddot x=-\beta\dot x-\kappa x+F_{\rm rand}(t),\ \ k_BT=\frac{D_p}{\beta}\ \Rightarrow\ k_BT_D=\frac{\hbar\Gamma}{2}
breaks: Sub-Doppler (Sisyphus) cooling and the recoil limit depend on optical pumping between internal states and on quantized photon momentum, which the damped-oscillator picture leaves out.
sources: Raab et al. (1987). "Trapping of Neutral Sodium Atoms with Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 59, 2631. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2631](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2631)

name: Damped oscillator: friction requires a bath
summary: Classical damping γ=ω₀/Q cannot come from a Hamiltonian for the oscillator alone. Quantum mechanically it comes from coupling to a bath (Caldeira–Leggett), which in the Markov limit gives a Lindblad equation with jump operators a and a†. The mean amplitude decays exactly as in the classical case, and fluctuation–dissipation adds thermal and zero-point noise.
map: \dot\rho=-\tfrac{i}{\hbar}[H,\rho]+\kappa(\bar n+1)\mathcal D[a]\rho+\kappa\bar n\,\mathcal D[a^\dagger]\rho,\ \ \kappa=\omega_0/Q,\ \ \langle a\rangle\propto e^{-\kappa t/2}
breaks: The Lindblad form needs weak coupling and a Markovian bath. Strongly damped or low-temperature quantum Brownian motion is non-Markovian and has no exact Lindblad description.
sources: Lindblad (1976). "On the generators of quantum dynamical semigroups". *Commun. Math. Phys.* 48, 119. [doi:10.1007/BF01608499](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01608499)

name: Critical damping is an exceptional point
summary: Written as a first-order system, the damped oscillator has a non-Hermitian 2×2 dynamical matrix. At critical damping, γ=2ω₀, its eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce at an exceptional point, whose Jordan-block signature is the t e^{−γt/2} solution. Coupled gain/loss oscillators undergo their PT-symmetry-breaking transition at the same kind of point.
breaks: Non-Hermitian quantum Hamiltonians describe post-selected or mean-field dynamics. Real quantum gain and loss add noise (Lindblad terms), which limits sensing enhanced by exceptional points.
sources: Bender & Boettcher (1998). "Real Spectra in Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians Having PT Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 5243. [arXiv:physics/9712001](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9712001)

name: Mechanical resonator driven into the quantum regime
summary: The mechanical element of an optomechanical system is a classical damped, driven oscillator whose frequency and damping are shifted by radiation pressure (optical spring, optical damping). Sideband cooling with κ<ω_m brings its mean phonon number below one, where zero-point motion and measurement backaction become observable.
map: m(\ddot x+\Gamma_m\dot x+\omega_m^2x)=F_{\rm th}+F_{\rm rad};\quad Q_mf_m>k_BT/h\ \text{for one coherent oscillation per thermal phonon}
breaks: Backaction noise, the standard quantum limit and nonclassical motional states are beyond the classical oscillator, which captures only the mean response.
sources: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg & Marquardt (2014). "Cavity optomechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 86, 1391. [arXiv:1303.0733](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.0733)

name: Coherent states: the quantum oscillator that moves classically
summary: A classically driven oscillator, or a classical current radiating into a mode, produces a coherent state: a displaced vacuum whose mean position and momentum follow the classical trajectory with constant minimum uncertainty. Glauber made it the reference classical state of light, with Poissonian photon counts.
breaks: The correspondence holds only for quadratic Hamiltonians, and vacuum-level quadrature noise remains. States with sub-Poissonian statistics or negative Wigner functions have no classical counterpart.
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)

name: Walking droplets: a hydrodynamic pilot-wave analogue
summary: Droplets bouncing on a bath vibrated vertically just below the Faraday (parametric) threshold are propelled by their own wave field. This macroscopic version of de Broglie's pilot wave shows quantized orbits, tunnelling-like crossings and wave-like statistics.
breaks: The wave lives in real 3D space, not configuration space, so the system is local and cannot produce entanglement or Bell violations. The early single- and double-slit interference claims (Couder & Fort 2006) were not reproduced in later controlled experiments.

name: Mathieu/Kapitza ↔ Floquet theory and high-frequency expansion
summary: Floquet theory began in classical mechanics, with Hill's lunar equation, Floquet (1883) and the Mathieu equation. The quasienergies of a quantum Floquet Hamiltonian correspond to Floquet exponents, and Kapitza's effective potential for the inverted pendulum is the leading term of the high-frequency expansion used in Floquet engineering.
breaks: The classical parametric instability becomes unbounded Floquet heating in interacting quantum systems. Many-body Floquet phases (time crystals, anomalous Floquet topology) have no single-oscillator counterpart.

name: Transmon as quantum pendulum and Duffing oscillator
summary: The transmon Hamiltonian is a quantum pendulum, and its eigenproblem in the charge basis is the Mathieu equation. Expanded about the minimum it is a weakly anharmonic (Duffing/Kerr) oscillator. Driven Duffing bistability gives bifurcation readout, and parametric pumping gives Josephson parametric amplifiers.

name: Paul trap: Mathieu stability and Kapitza pseudopotential
summary: An ion in an RF quadrupole field obeys the Mathieu equation and is confined when (a,q) lies inside the first stability region. Its slow secular motion sits in a ponderomotive pseudopotential, the same averaging that stabilizes Kapitza's inverted pendulum, with residual micromotion at the drive frequency.

name: Degenerate parametric amplification → squeezing
summary: Pumping an oscillator at twice its frequency amplifies one quadrature and de-amplifies the other. Classically this squeezes the thermal noise of a mechanical resonator (Rugar & Grütter 1991). In optics and Josephson circuits the same phase-sensitive gain squeezes vacuum fluctuations, which gravitational-wave interferometers inject to beat the shot-noise limit.
map: \hat X_1\to e^{r}\hat X_1,\ \ \hat X_2\to e^{-r}\hat X_2;\ \ \Delta X_2^2=\tfrac14e^{-2r}\ (\text{vacuum}:\ \tfrac14)
breaks: Below threshold, classical parametric squeezing inside a resonator is capped at 3 dB and never goes below zero-point noise. Sub-vacuum noise is the quantum resource.
sources: Caves (1981). "Quantum-mechanical noise in an interferometer". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 1693. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693)

name: Larmor precession: spin behaves as a gyroscope
summary: A magnetic moment μ=γS in a field feels a torque that makes its angular momentum precess, like a gyroscope under gravity. Because the spin Hamiltonian is linear in S, the Heisenberg equation for ⟨S⟩ is exactly this classical precession, which is the basis of the Bloch equations, NMR/MRI and spin-qubit control.
breaks: Only the mean precesses classically; individual measurements give quantized ±ħ/2. The electron's g≈2 also differs from the gyromagnetic ratio q/2m of a classical rotating charge.

name: Classical optics as the coherent-state limit
summary: Classical wave optics is reproduced exactly by quantized light in coherent states: first-order interference, diffraction and imaging depend only on mode functions and the mean field, so quantum features appear only in photon counting and higher-order correlations.
map: |\alpha\rangle:\ \langle\hat E^{(+)}\rangle=\mathcal E\,\alpha\,u(\mathbf r)e^{-i\omega t},\ g^{(1)}\ \text{classical},\ g^{(2)}=1
breaks: Fails for Fock, squeezed and entangled states and for g^(2)(0)<1 (antibunching), which no classical field can produce.
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)

name: Coherence functions: classical to Glauber
summary: The classical degree of coherence g^(1) and the Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity correlation g^(2) become Glauber's normally ordered field correlators. Thermal bunching g^(2)(0)=2 appears in both theories; antibunching g^(2)(0)<1 is the purely quantum signature.
map: g^{(2)}(\tau)=\frac{\langle\hat E^-(t)\hat E^-(t+\tau)\hat E^+(t+\tau)\hat E^+(t)\rangle}{\langle\hat E^-\hat E^+\rangle^2};\ \text{classical } g^{(2)}(0)\ge1
breaks: Classical stochastic fields obey g^(2)(0)>=1 and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities that quantum light can violate.
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)
Kimble, Dagenais & Mandel (1977). "Photon Antibunching in Resonance Fluorescence". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 39, 691. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.691](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.691)

name: Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy: eikonal ↔ action
summary: Fermat's principle and the eikonal equation are the short-wavelength limit of wave optics, just as Hamilton–Jacobi mechanics is the ħ→0 limit of quantum mechanics. Schrödinger built wave mechanics by completing Hamilton's analogy, and WKB semiclassics is the eikonal method applied to matter waves.
map: |\nabla\mathcal S_{\rm opt}|^2=n^2\ \leftrightarrow\ |\nabla S|^2=2m(E-V),\ \ k_0\mathcal S_{\rm opt}\leftrightarrow S/\hbar
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Atom interferometry: optical interferometers for atoms
summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers copy the Mach–Zehnder geometry, with laser pulses as beam splitters and mirrors, and Ramsey's separated-field method is a two-slit experiment in time. They measure g, rotations and h/m and test the equivalence principle.
breaks: Atoms are massive, with quadratic dispersion and internal states. Their phase picks up gravity and photon recoil, and their beam splitters are coherent internal-state transitions rather than passive optics.

name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as free-particle propagator
summary: Fresnel diffraction sums secondary wavelets weighted by e^{ikr}, just as Feynman's path integral sums e^{iS/ħ}. The paraxial Fresnel kernel is the free-particle propagator with z↔t and k↔m/ħ, and stationary phase picks out rays, the optical counterpart of classical paths.
map: K=\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar t}}e^{\frac{im(x-x')^2}{2\hbar t}}\leftrightarrow h=\sqrt{\frac{k}{2\pi iz}}e^{\frac{ik(x-x')^2}{2z}},\ \frac{m}{\hbar t}\leftrightarrow\frac{k}{z}
breaks: The optical 'time' z is a spatial coordinate, and the mapping fails beyond the paraxial, scalar approximation (obliquity factors, vector diffraction).
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Beam splitters: Mach–Zehnder to Hong–Ou–Mandel
summary: The beam-splitter unitary is the same for classical field amplitudes and for photon creation operators, so a single photon reproduces classical fringes. Two identical photons bunch (the HOM dip) with visibility up to 100% against a classical maximum of 50%, which is how single-photon sources are certified as indistinguishable.
breaks: Two-photon interference depends on number states and photon indistinguishability; no classical field gives HOM visibility above 50%.
sources: Hong, Ou & Mandel (1987). "Measurement of subpicosecond time intervals between two photons by interference". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 59, 2044. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2044](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2044)

name: Interferometer shot noise and squeezed-vacuum injection
summary: With coherent light, a Michelson or Mach–Zehnder interferometer's phase sensitivity is shot-noise limited at 1/√N. Caves showed this noise enters as vacuum fluctuations through the unused port, so injecting squeezed vacuum there beats the limit, as LIGO and Virgo now do.
sources: Caves (1981). "Quantum-mechanical noise in an interferometer". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 1693. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693)

name: Polarization qubits and polarization entanglement
summary: Jones vectors are qubit states and wave plates are SU(2) gates. Photon pairs entangled in polarization are therefore the main platform for entanglement witnesses, state tomography and Bell tests.
sources: Aspect, Dalibard & Roger (1982). "Experimental Test of Bell's Inequalities Using Time-Varying Analyzers". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 49, 1804. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1804](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1804)
Horodecki et al. (2009). "Quantum entanglement". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 865. [arXiv:quant-ph/0702225](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0702225)

name: Photon spin and orbital angular momentum
summary: Circularly polarized light carries spin angular momentum ±ħ per photon (Beth 1936), and Laguerre–Gauss beams with phase e^{iℓφ} carry orbital angular momentum ℓħ. Transfer to atoms follows the Δm selection rules, and both degrees of freedom serve as qudit encodings.
breaks: The massless photon has only helicity ±1 (no m=0 state), and the split into spin and orbital parts is gauge-dependent outside the paraxial regime.

name: Pancharatnam phase on the Poincaré sphere
summary: Pancharatnam (1956) found that light taken around a closed cycle of polarization states gains a phase of minus half the solid angle it encloses on the Poincaré sphere. This is Berry's spin-1/2 phase, found in optics decades earlier, and it is now used in Pancharatnam–Berry geometric-phase metasurfaces.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Polarization coherency matrix = qubit density matrix
summary: The 2×2 coherency matrix of partially polarized light is a density matrix whose Stokes parameters are the Bloch-vector components. The degree of polarization is the Bloch-vector length, wave plates act as unitaries, and depolarizing elements (Mueller matrices) act as quantum channels.
breaks: Classical partial polarization is an ensemble average over field fluctuations; beams that are nonseparable in polarization and spatial mode ('classical entanglement') show no nonlocality.

name: Microwave billiards as quantum-chaos simulators
summary: Below the cutoff of the second vertical mode, a flat microwave cavity's TM modes obey the 2D Helmholtz equation, which is the Schrödinger equation of a particle in a hard-wall billiard. Measured resonance spectra test random-matrix level statistics (GOE for chaotic shapes) and wavefunction scarring.
breaks: Holds only for the lowest TM modes of thin cavities. Absorption broadens the levels, and time reversal can be broken only by adding ferrites.
sources: Bohigas, Giannoni & Schmit (1984). "Characterization of Chaotic Quantum Spectra and Universality of Level Fluctuation Laws". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 1. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1)

name: Transmission-line resonators as circuit-QED cavities
summary: Superconducting coplanar-waveguide resonators, which are classical transmission lines with standing-wave modes, supply the photon modes of circuit QED. Their tiny transverse mode volume makes vacuum fields large enough for a transmon to reach strong coupling.
map: \omega_n=\frac{n\pi v_p}{\ell},\ v_p=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_\ell C_\ell}},\ \hat H=\hbar\omega_r(\hat a^\dagger\hat a+\tfrac12),\ V_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{\hbar\omega_r/2C}
sources: Wallraff et al. (2004). "Strong coupling of a single photon to a superconducting qubit using circuit quantum electrodynamics". *Nature* 431, 162. [doi:10.1038/nature02851](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02851)
